extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, judges, and law students
extracted.subtask_description: Standards for determining patentable subject-matter: usefulness, unity/diversity of invention, and how combination claims and separate claims should be treated. Explains classes of machine-related inventions and how claim scope and infringement differ across them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Licensee by operation of law (statutory benefit)
rubrics_metrics.description: To entitle a person to claim the benefit of the statute as a licensee by operation of law, he must be a purchaser or one who has used the patented invention before the patent was issued, by a license or grant or by the consent of the inventor, and not be a purchaser under a mere wrong-doer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What will amount to such a license, grant, or consent illustrated by case: an employee who, while receiving wages, made experiments at employer's expense in the employer's manufactory, whose wages were increased due to the useful result, made the article, permitted employer to use it without compensation or demand, and then obtained a patent — such unmolested and notorious prior use brought case within statute. (Example: §104 and accompanying case discussion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness requirement (positive utility)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention, to be the subject of a patent, must be 'useful.' This utility is the statutory description of the class of inventions which can be valid patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish positive (statutory) utility from comparative/relative utility used in novelty inquiries. The law requires only that the invention be capable of some beneficial practical use and not be injurious to morals, health, or public order; the degree of utility (large or small) is not relevant to statutory satisfaction. If trifling or frivolous, the invention may be unprofitable, but the statute merely requires capability of use and lack of noxious tendency. (See §105–106 and cited authorities.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility vs. false suggestion / misleading specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Inquiry whether some part of a thing claimed or described in a specification is useless to the intended effect is a question of whether the patent is void for a false suggestion or calculated to mislead the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate the statutory usefulness requirement with isolated questions as to whether a claimed part is necessary to produce an effect — such issues probe the accuracy and honesty of the specification rather than statutory utility. (See §105 discussion.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of invention (general rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The terms of the patent acts do not admit of distinct inventions as the subject of a single patent; the subject-matter must be one invention or discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where distinct inventions exist, the party ordinarily must take out separate patents. Historic dicta warn against a single patent embracing various distinct improvements or inventions (Barrett v. Hall), though later cases refine exceptions. (See §107–109.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Exception — connected inventions/subserve common end
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinct inventions that are capable of being used in connection and to subserve a common end may be included in one patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have held that when separate devices were contrived with a view of being used conjointly and to subserve a common end, their capability of separate use does not prevent their being embraced in one patent; wrongful use of either may infringe pro tanto. (Illustrated by Emerson v. Hogg, Wyeth v. Stone, and later Supreme Court rulings.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification: machine as entire new machine (Clifford's first class)
rubrics_metrics.description: First class embraces inventions which embrace the entire machine, as a car for a railway or a sewing-machine; such inventions are the machine itself as an entirety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the patent is for the whole machine as a new entirety, any person who, without license, makes or uses any portion of the machine is an infringer. The patentee holds exclusive right to make, use, and vend the entire machine. (See §111a, first class.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification: patent to one or more elements (Clifford's second class)
rubrics_metrics.description: Second class embraces patents for one or more elements of a machine (but not the entire machine), e.g., a coulter of a plow or divider of a reaping-machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such patents others may make, use, or vend the remainder of the machine and may employ the patented element only if it is not 'substantially different' from the claimed element. Infringement requires substantial similarity of the element. (See §111a, second class.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification: new element plus new combination (Clifford's third class)
rubrics_metrics.description: Third class embraces inventions combining a new element with a new combination of previously known elements; the patentee's property consists in both the new element and the new combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No one may lawfully make, use, or vend a machine containing the patented new element or the patented new combination; however the machine without the improvements may be made or used. (See §111a, third class.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification: new combination of old elements (Clifford's fourth class)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fourth class embraces inventions where all elements are old and the invention consists in their new combination producing a new and useful result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Property is commensurate with the invention (i.e., limited to the new combination). Others may independently arrive at and use a substantially different combination even if it obtains the same result. Most modern improvements fall in this class. (See §111a, fourth class.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a patentable combination
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination in machinery is a new union of elemental parts not before brought together in that kind of machine, producing a method of operation differing from what had been done before in that kind of machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements of the combination may be new or old; successive action of elements that contributes to a practical result suffices (not necessary to act simultaneously). It is not requisite to include in the claim every part necessary to the machine's action, except as they enter into the mode of combining and arranging the elements. (See §111 and cited cases like Buck v. Hermance and Forbush v. Cook.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical-result test for combinations and improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: If changes in an old machine adapt it to a new and valuable use not known before, and it actually produces a new and useful result, it may be patented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts assess whether the change actually adapts the machine to a novel valuable use and yields a new useful result. The patent requirement is satisfied if the combination is new and the machine is capable of beneficial use for its designed purpose; the law does not require the improvement to supersede all others. (See §111b and Justice Clifford's statements in Seymour v. Osborne.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive step vs. mechanical skill in combinations
rubrics_metrics.description: A defense to a combination patent is that the combining of old parts involved merely the skill of an intelligent mechanic rather than invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts examine prior art and whether prior machines embodied similar features; if the combination would have been obvious to a skilled mechanic, it may not require patentable invention. The treatise recounts how lower courts and the Supreme Court evaluated evidence in Seymour v. Osborne (e.g., Piatt's machine) to distinguish invention from mere mechanical skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction affects validity and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether claims are presented as claims for separate machines, as combinations, or both affects validity and what the patent covers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Evans (claims separate machines and conjointly) created doubts as to regularity under general patent law; Wyeth v. Stone and Emerson v. Hogg show that claims for separate machines and combinations may be sustained when the devices relate to a common purpose. Drafting should make clear whether claim is for combination or for distinct machines, because that will determine infringement and potential invalidity for embracing more than one subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pro tanto infringement for partial wrongful use
rubrics_metrics.description: Where distinct inventions are united in one patent and are capable of separate use, the wrongful use of either machine is a violation of the patent right pro tanto.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When separate machines or devices are contrived to subserve a common end and are embraced in one patent, using any one without license can constitute partial infringement proportional to the part used. (See Emerson v. Hogg and related discussion.)
